title: Rate limiting and cost controls
lesson_status_html: Published lesson 16 of 26Complete the lesson and quick check, then record your progress.

sections.heading: 1. The attack
sections.html:
Running example: ExampleAir's partner API, limited to 100 requests per minute. Company names are fictional. The limit is documented, implemented, and returns 429 when it fires.

The first attack does not exceed it. A caller sends 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00, and both batches are inside their minute. Two hundred requests in two seconds, from a service that promised a hundred a minute, and nothing was violated.

The other three do not even try. They stay under the limit and get what they want anyway, because a limit on the number of requests is not a limit on cost, on duration, on how many identities a caller may hold, or on how many of your instances are counting separately.

OWASP puts the consequence plainly in API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption, which names the cost side of this directly: exploitation leads to "operational costs increase such as those related to the infrastructure due to higher CPU demand, increasing cloud storage needs, etc."

The callerFixed windowSliding windowToken bucket
Sends 100 in a minuteAllowed, as intendedAllowedAllowed
Sends 100 either side of the boundary200 in two seconds100101
Sends 100 in one instant, from idleAllowed onceAllowed onceAllowed, by design
Sends 100 requests that each cost 50 times moreAllowedAllowedAllowed
Sends one a second for a day86400, none refused8640086400
Holds fifty identities5000, each within its limit50005000
Reaches four instances counting separately400400400

The choice of algorithm settles one row. The last four are settled by what you count, whose it is, and where the counter lives, and those are decisions no algorithm makes for you.

sections.heading: 2. Why it works
sections.html:
Three algorithms, and what each one permits at its worst

The differences are small to implement and large in effect, and the useful way to compare them is by their worst moment rather than their average.

  • Fixed window. Count per calendar minute, reset at the boundary. Its worst moment is the boundary, where two full windows are two seconds apart, so the observed peak is twice the limit in an arbitrarily short time. Cheap to implement, and the peak is the part people do not picture.
  • Sliding window. Count the requests in the last sixty seconds, whenever the request arrives. There is no boundary, so there is no boundary burst. It costs more memory, because you are keeping timestamps rather than a counter.
  • Token bucket. A bucket of some capacity refilling at some rate. Capacity is the burst you are prepared to serve and rate is the average you are prepared to sustain, and separating those two numbers is the point. Its worst moment is a full bucket, which permits the whole capacity at once, on purpose.

The token bucket's row in the table above says 101 rather than 100, and that is not a rounding error: it is the full bucket at 12:00:59 plus the 1.67 tokens that refilled by 12:01:00. Watching a limiter produce a number you did not predict is the fastest way to find out what it actually enforces.

Four things a request count does not count

Cost. A request that reads one row and a request that runs a report are one request each. OWASP's prevention list starts with the resource side, "use a solution that makes it easy to limit memory, CPU, number of restarts, file descriptors, and processes such as Containers / Serverless code", and continues with the pricing side, "configure spending limits for all service providers/API integrations. When setting spending limits is not possible, billing alerts should be configured instead". Between those two sits the API's own answer: charge each request what it costs and limit the total.

Duration. A rate limit constrains a minute. It says nothing about a day, and one request a second for a day is 86,400 requests without a single refusal. If what you care about is the total, a rate limit is not the control; a quota is, and module 11 is where the number comes from.

Identity. A per-caller limit is exactly as strong as the cost of becoming another caller. Where identities are free, the limit is a formality. OWASP's advice here is to tune by endpoint rather than globally: "rate limiting should be fine tuned based on the business needs. Some API Endpoints might require stricter policies", and specifically to "limit/throttle how many times or how often a single API client/user can execute a single operation (e.g. validate an OTP, or request password recovery)".

Where the counter lives. Four instances with local counters enforce four times your limit, and they do it silently, because each one is correct about what it saw. This is module 11's shared-store argument in a second place, and it is the one most likely to be true in your system right now.

What to say when you refuse

429 is defined in RFC 6585 section 4, not in the core HTTP semantics document, and its definition is short and worth reading in full. It "indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time", the response "SHOULD include details explaining the condition, and MAY include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait before making a new request", and "responses with the 429 status code MUST NOT be stored by a cache". That last one is a requirement people miss and a cache will happily ignore on your behalf.

The same section says something more interesting: servers "are not required to use the 429 status code; when limiting resource usage, it may be more appropriate to just drop connections, or take other steps", because "when a server is under attack or just receiving a very large number of requests from a single party, responding to each with a 429 status code will consume resources". A polite refusal is still work. Under attack, the cheapest response is the right one.

On telling clients their remaining quota: there is no standard. The IETF work on RateLimit header fields, draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers, reached revision 11 in May 2026 and is still an Internet-Draft, with a "Not ready" early review on the previous revision in January 2026. Emitting those headers is reasonable and common. Calling them standard is not, and a client that depends on them is depending on your implementation.

The whole system

TrafficBoundedBounded by designTwice the limit

sections.heading: 3. The control
sections.html:
1. Pick the algorithm from the worst moment you will accept. Fixed window if double the limit in two seconds is fine. Token bucket if you want to permit a burst and name its size. Sliding window if you want neither.
  2. Count cost, not requests, wherever requests differ by more than a small factor. Assign each operation a weight and limit the total weight.
  3. Add a quota beside the rate. The rate protects the system from a moment. The quota protects the business from a day, and the number comes from whoever knows what the flow is worth.
  4. Decide what the limit is per, and price the alternative. Per caller, per account, per endpoint, per tenant. If a second identity is free, the per-caller limit is decoration.
  5. Put the counter in a store every instance shares, and test it against a second instance. Four local counters enforce four times your limit.
  6. Limit the resources underneath as well: memory, CPU, processes, file descriptors, execution timeouts. OWASP names these first for a reason, because they bound what a request can cost even when your accounting is wrong.
  7. Set spending limits on every paid integration, or billing alerts where limits are not available.
  8. Refuse cheaply. 429 with a short body, no caching, and where the volume makes even that expensive, drop instead.

sections.heading_text: 4. Defaults and when to change them
sections.html:
DecisionStarting defaultChange it when
AlgorithmToken bucket, with capacity and rate stated separatelySliding window where no burst is acceptable. Fixed window only where double the limit in two seconds genuinely does not matter.
What is countedA cost weight per operation, not a requestPlain request counts are fine where every operation costs about the same. Measure before believing that.
Rate and quotaBoth: a per-minute rate and a per-day quotaOne of them alone leaves either the moment or the total unbounded.
ScopePer authenticated caller, plus a global ceilingPer IP where callers are anonymous, knowing it is weak. Per tenant where one tenant's traffic can starve another's.
Sensitive operationsA stricter, separate limitOWASP names one-time-password validation and password recovery specifically. Add anything that costs money or sends a message.
Where the counter livesA store every instance sharesNever per instance. Test the limit against a second instance, not a second request.
Resource limitsMemory, CPU, processes, descriptors and timeouts, set at the platformThese bound the damage when the accounting above is wrong, which it will be at least once.
Paid integrationsA spending limit, or a billing alert where limits are unavailableThis is the control that stops a bug becoming an invoice.
The refusal429, small body, uncacheableUnder volume, dropping is cheaper and RFC 6585 explicitly permits it.
Telling clients their quotaRateLimit headers if you like, documented as yoursThey are still an Internet-Draft. Do not describe them to partners as a standard.

sections.heading: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.heading_text: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
Proves: that a single identified caller cannot exceed a stated number of weighted operations in a stated period, as counted by a store all your instances share.

Doesn't prove: that your total load is bounded, that your bill is bounded, or that a determined caller is bounded. Each of those needs something else: a global ceiling, a spending limit, and a view of how expensive a second identity is.

A limit is a claim about a number you chose to count. "100 per minute" is precise about requests and silent about work, about the day, about how many accounts one person has, and about how many copies of the counter exist. Every incident in this area is somebody discovering which of those four the limit was never about.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
For each limit you publish:

  • The worst-case burst is written down, and it matches what the algorithm actually permits.
  • A test drives traffic across the window boundary and asserts the number allowed.
  • A test drives the same traffic through two instances and asserts the shared counter held.
  • Operations carry cost weights, or there is a measurement showing they cost the same.
  • A daily or monthly quota exists beside the per-minute rate.
  • Sensitive operations have their own stricter limit, tested separately.
  • Platform resource limits exist: memory, CPU, processes, descriptors, execution timeout.
  • Every paid integration has a spending limit or a billing alert, and somebody receives it.
  • 429 responses are not cached, and there is a test that proves it.

sections.heading: 7. Lab
sections.html:
Download labs/rate_limit_lab.py. It needs nothing beyond Python 3.

Windows              macOS and Linux
py -3 labs/rate_limit_lab.py    python3 labs/rate_limit_lab.py

There is no python3 command on a default Windows install, so use py -3 there. The three limiters are real implementations, about ten lines each. The clock is a number the file increments, so nothing sleeps and every run produces the same output.

$ python3 labs/rate_limit_lab.py
the stated limit is 100 requests per 60 seconds

Part A: a fixed window, counted per calendar minute.
 1. 100 requests at t=59                               100 allowed
 2. 100 more at t=60                                   100 allowed
 3. allowed in those two seconds                       200
 4. the same traffic expressed as a rate               6000 per minute
 5. the 101st request inside one window                refused

Part B: a sliding window over the last 60 seconds.
 6. 100 requests at t=59                               100 allowed
 7. 100 more at t=60                                   0 allowed
 8. allowed in those two seconds                       100
 9. a request at t=119, once the first batch ages out  allowed

Part C: a token bucket, capacity 100, refilling 100 per minute.
10. 100 requests at t=0, from a full bucket            100 allowed
11. one more at t=0                                    refused
12. one at t=1, after 1.67 tokens refill               allowed
13. a caller sending 1 per second for 600 seconds      600 allowed
14. seconds to wait after draining it                  1

Part D: what a request-rate limit does not bound.
15. 100 cheap requests, 1 unit each                    100 units
16. 100 expensive requests, 50 units each              5000 units
17. the same expensive traffic, cost-weighted at 50    4 allowed
18. 1 request per second for a day                     86400 allowed
19. any of them refused                                0
20. 50 identities, each inside its own limit           5000 allowed
21. one caller across 4 instances with local counters  400 allowed
22. the same traffic against one shared counter        100 allowed

all lab checks passed

Checks 1 to 4 are the boundary. Both batches are inside their minute, the limiter is correct on its own terms, and the observed rate over the span is sixty times the published one. Check 4 is the number to put in front of anyone who says a fixed window is fine.

Checks 15 to 17 are the cost argument as arithmetic. The same hundred requests are a hundred units or five thousand depending on what they do, and the limiter cannot tell. Check 17 weights each request at 50 and the same traffic yields four accepted requests over a hundred seconds instead of a hundred, which is what charging for work rather than for requests looks like.

Check 18 is the one that changes how people write limits. Eighty-six thousand requests, not one of them refused, every single one inside a limit that was set deliberately. If the number you actually care about is the daily total, the per-minute rate was never measuring it.

Checks 21 and 22 are the same caller and the same traffic against four local counters and one shared one. Four hundred against a hundred, and every instance was right about what it saw.

Try next:

  • Run the boundary burst through all three limiters and compare. The token bucket allows 101, not 100. Work out where the extra one comes from before reading on: it is the 1.67 tokens that refilled between t=59 and t=60.
  • Change TokenBucket's capacity to 10 while leaving the rate alone. The sustained rate is unchanged and the burst is a tenth. That is the knob a fixed or sliding window does not give you.
  • Give SlidingWindow a limit of 100 and send 50 requests of cost 2. Then send 100 of cost 1. Both are 100 units and only one of them is 100 requests.
  • Write down the per-minute rate and the per-day quota for one endpoint you own. If only one of the two exists, you have found this module's point in your own system.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
Your limit is 100 per minute on a fixed window. What is the most a caller can send in two seconds?

Two hundred, by sending a full window's worth just before the boundary and another immediately after. Both batches are within their own minute, so nothing was violated. If that peak matters, use a sliding window, or a token bucket with a capacity you chose on purpose.

Why is a token bucket's burst not a bug?

Because capacity and rate are two separate numbers and the burst is the capacity. That is the feature: you can permit a client to catch up after being idle while still bounding the sustained rate. The mistake is not setting a capacity, it is not knowing what you set it to.

Every caller is within the limit and the bill has tripled. What happened?

Probably one of three things. Requests are not equal and something expensive got popular, so limit the cost rather than the count. Or the total over a day was never bounded, because a per-minute rate says nothing about a day. Or a paid integration has no spending limit, which OWASP lists as its own prevention item.

Your rate limiter is correct and callers exceed the limit anyway. Where would you look first?

At where the counter lives. If each service instance counts locally, your effective limit is the published one multiplied by the number of instances, and every instance is behaving correctly. Test the limit by sending traffic to two instances, not by sending two requests.

Quick check

sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • Standard"Implement a limit on how often a client can interact with the API within a defined timeframe (rate limiting)." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
  • Standard"Rate limiting should be fine tuned based on the business needs. Some API Endpoints might require stricter policies." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
  • Standard"Limit/throttle how many times or how often a single API client/user can execute a single operation (e.g. validate an OTP, or request password recovery)." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
  • Standard"Use a solution that makes it easy to limit memory, CPU, number of restarts, file descriptors, and processes such as Containers / Serverless code." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
  • Standard"Configure spending limits for all service providers/API integrations. When setting spending limits is not possible, billing alerts should be configured instead." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
  • Standard429 Too Many Requests "indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time", the response "SHOULD include details explaining the condition, and MAY include a Retry-After header", and responses with it "MUST NOT be stored by a cache". RFC 6585 section 4.
  • StandardServers "are not required to use the 429 status code; when limiting resource usage, it may be more appropriate to just drop connections, or take other steps", because responding to each request consumes resources. RFC 6585 section 4.
  • BaselineThere is no standard for RateLimit response headers. draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers reached revision 11 in May 2026 and remains an Internet-Draft. Emit them if useful, and document them as yours.
  • BaselineChoose the algorithm by its worst moment, and write that number down beside the published limit.
  • BaselineLimit weighted cost rather than request count wherever operations differ by more than a small factor.
  • BaselinePublish a rate and a quota. The rate bounds a moment, the quota bounds a period.
  • BaselineHold counters in a store every instance shares, and test against a second instance rather than a second request.
  • BaselineState what the limit is per, and know the cost of obtaining another one of those.
  • OptionReturn Retry-After, defined in RFC 9110 section 10.2.3, on refusals where you want clients to back off predictably rather than retry immediately.
  • OptionDrop rather than answer when the volume makes answering the expensive part. RFC 6585 permits this explicitly.

sections.heading: Review checklist items
sections.html:
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • Counters are held in a store every instance shares Tested by driving traffic through two instances. Local counters multiply the published limit by the instance count.
  • The worst-case burst is written down and matches the algorithm A fixed window permits twice the limit across its boundary. A token bucket permits its capacity. Test the boundary.
  • Expensive operations are limited by cost, not by request count Or there is a measurement showing operations cost about the same.
  • A quota exists beside the rate A per-minute limit does not bound a day. One request a second is 86,400 with nothing refused.
  • Every paid integration has a spending limit or a billing alert And somebody receives the alert. OWASP lists this as its own prevention item.
  • Sensitive operations have their own stricter limits One-time-password validation, password recovery, anything that sends a message or spends money.
  • Platform resource limits are set Memory, CPU, processes, file descriptors and execution timeouts, so a wrong limit is not an unbounded one.
  • 429 responses are uncacheable and cheap RFC 6585 requires they not be stored by a cache, and permits dropping instead when answering is itself the cost.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.html:
• OWASP API Security Top 10 2023, API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption.
  • RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes, April 2012. Section 4, 429 Too Many Requests.
  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics, June 2022. Section 10.2.3 defines Retry-After.
  • draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers: RateLimit header fields for HTTP. Revision 11, May 2026. An active Internet-Draft, not a standard.
Part of API Security in the Age of AI. Examples use fictional companies and the reserved .example domain. No real keys appear on this site.
